notes.subject: the base commit
notes.note: R-f makes 2f8712a the tie-breaker, so every baseline record in this artifact is a MEASUREMENT taken by driving a `git worktree` at that commit with its own `npm ci`, never a guess. A scenario whose baseline has not been measured carries `baseline: null` and a step whose response has not been recorded carries `response: null`. Neither is ever stood in for by a plausible value: an invented status would make the parity gate pass against a fiction.

notes.subject: provenance
notes.note: Not in this file. It lives in the sibling `corpus.json.provenance.json`, which capture.js always writes beside the corpus: the analysed worktree and its git HEAD, this tool's own HEAD, the manifest, the seeding and object-store summary, the fixture profiles and the launcher options. Keeping it out of here is what lets the corpus stay diff-clean - a re-capture on a different day changes the provenance and should not therefore rewrite every scenario. Read the two together: a corpus without its sidecar does not say which tree it measured, and is not parity evidence.

notes.subject: capture status
notes.note: NOT YET CAPTURED. All 383 scenarios in this file are DEFINITIONS with `baseline: null`; none carries a captured baseline, and `summary.captured` is false. The definitions are the authored, reviewable part - route, identity, Accept mode, intent, payload, fixture profile and step order are design decisions - and they are emitted by capture.js's own builder, so the two artifacts cannot disagree about the schema. Running `node test/parity/capture.js --app <worktree at 2f8712a>` replaces the `scenarios` array with the driven records and rewrites the blocks below from what it observed.

notes.subject: the single-pass capture blocker, measured
notes.note: A capture of all 383 scenarios in ONE pass does not complete at 2f8712a, and the cause is in the application rather than in the tooling. Route `POST /api/admin/user/{userId}` reaches `admin.updateUser`, whose `User.findById` callback does `if (err) return request.fail(err)` [lib/controllers/admin.js:158-160]; `request.fail` hands the Error to `h.response` [lib/util/routeParser.js:510], hapi asserts "Cannot wrap an error", and the UNCAUGHT async exception exits the process. Measured three times, including with that one scenario driven alone against a fresh database and a fresh server, where it records ECONNRESET in under 20ms. Every case driven after it records a transport failure that means nothing. Capture around it in coherent segments and record that scenario on its own; do NOT commit post-crash transport failures as baselines, and do not merge passes that ran on different ports - absolute Location values embed the port - or on differently mutated databases, which was measured to lose the seeded user session and turn the authenticated /login 500 into a 200.

notes.subject: the schema version key
notes.note: `schema` and `version` are the same integer. `schema` is the key capture.js writes and is the one to read; `version` is an alias carried for readers that expect it, and a re-capture emits `schema` alone. Three further fields in this file are likewise not written by capture.js and exist because they are what a reader checks before a capture has run: the per-scenario `baseline`, the `unreachableReason` on the one scenario that cannot be driven, and the `expectedDeviation` on the one approved deviation. A capture replaces the scenario array wholesale, so it drops all three; their absence is itself the signal that the records are measured.

notes.subject: the shape of a step before and after capture
notes.note: Before capture a step carries its SPEC - label, method, target, accept, payload and the substitutions that materialized the path - plus `response: null`. When capture.js drives it, the step is replaced by {label, request, response}, where `request` is what was actually sent. Both shapes keep `label`, which is what a sequence is reported by.

notes.subject: the one approved deviation
notes.note: Exactly one scenario carries `expectedDeviation`: quirk.reply-chain.never-settles.image-download. The image branch of the file download never settles at baseline, and AAP 0.7 decides the collision with "every route serves" in favour of serving, so the target answers 200 with the stream. A replay must report that as an APPROVED CHANGE, not a failure. The four header-resolved chains carry no marker and must not become collateral damage of that decision - their responses are expected to be identical. `error-edge.asset-from-url.transport-refused` is also an expected timeout but is NOT a deviation: that route is left unsettled in the target too, so its timeout is preserved behaviour.

notes.subject: volatile data
notes.note: Nothing avoidable is left volatile in a `request`. Every id in every driven path is a frozen fixture id from test/parity/seed.js, so no path carries a generated id and none is left as a `{template}`. No timestamp and no cookie value appears in a request: the cookie jar is established at run time by logging the seeded identities in, and session cookie VALUES are replaced by their digest at capture time. Anything still volatile is enumerated in the notes capture.js contributes below, and each entry there is a weakening that has to be justified in docs/baseline-parity.md rather than assumed.

notes.subject: reCAPTCHA outcomes 3 to 6
notes.note: Unreachable over HTTP, and deliberately not chased. Under NODE_ENV=test the verify helper short-circuits on the isTest flag before any HTTP happens, so the 200, non-200, transport-failure and malformed-JSON branches cannot be reached through a route however the fixture is configured. They are exercised by direct module-level invocation in the fixture harness instead. Adding a reCAPTCHA secret to the overlay would not help - the short-circuit is on the environment, not on the secret - so none is added.

notes.subject: the fifth auth-scheme outcome
notes.note: The "Auth error" branch needs the user lookup itself to fail, which no HTTP request can cause. It is recorded as an unreachable scenario with that reason rather than simulated, because anything that could be driven from here would reach a different branch and be captured as though it were this one.

notes.subject: the Google client configuration
notes.note: Both OAuth handlers short-circuit without a configured client, and the server overlay does not declare one. This tool injects a fake client as an explicit top NODE_CONFIG layer so the OAuth branches are reachable at all. The values are not credentials: the token and profile endpoints are intercepted at the module boundary, so nothing authenticates against anything.

notes.subject: the OAuth existing-user identity
notes.note: The http fixture's seeding contract asks that its `existing` identity be seeded as a user, and the seeder does not seed it. The alignment call the fixture offers runs only inside the server process, and its environment contract has no identity variable, so neither artifact can be aligned from here. Rather than edit a sibling artifact, the existing-user branch is reached as a two-step sequence in which the new-user branch creates the account first. The gap is real and is recorded here; closing it in the seeder would make the sequence unnecessary but would not change what it captures.

notes.subject: cookie values
notes.note: The one value normalized at capture time. Session cookie values are already in the enumerated volatile set, so recording a digest instead of the value loses nothing that could have been compared, while keeping live session tokens out of a committed artifact. Every attribute that IS compared - name, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Path, Domain, Max-Age, and the presence and day horizon of Expires - is preserved in full, because the Expires horizon is the only way a silent no-op in the private-field cookie patch can be detected.

notes.subject: the cache-prefix timestamp in rendered asset URLs
notes.note: The one volatile value embedded in comparable HTML, and the only thing that differed between two consecutive captures of the same tree once cookies, Date and raw elapsed times are set aside. Every rendered page carries asset URLs of the form /cache-prefix-<epoch-millis>/<assetType>/<path>, because the string helper that builds them inlines the clock at RENDER time - it is not read from configuration, so no overlay can pin it and no fixture can make it stable. Measured: 20 of 242 read-only responses differed on this and on nothing else. It is a timestamp, so it is inside the enumerated volatile set, but it sits inside an href that is otherwise compared exactly - so a replay that does not normalize this pattern will report a difference on every rendered page. Normalize the digits between "/cache-prefix-" and the following "/" and compare the rest of the URL exactly; the prefix itself is configured and IS worth comparing.

notes.subject: redirects
notes.note: Not followed. A Location header is part of the surface under comparison, and following it would replace the measurement with its consequence. Note that the two redirect mechanisms differ and both appear here: the parser builds ABSOLUTE locations from the configured url, while the 401 branch of the error extension emits a RELATIVE /login.

expectation.description: the queryless case answers 200 with an empty data list, and the query-bearing case answers 200

notes: step 1 is driven BARE, where the malformed injected URL is not a query at all: the path misses the API route entirely, is served by the static catch-all, and the result carries no `data`, so the route answers 200 with an empty list and the trinket listing is never invoked

the ASSERTED invariant is the queryless empty list, because that is the measured, documented baseline behaviour and it is what a conversion would accidentally fix by passing the folder through in both cases

the pair is recorded so replay.js compares BOTH bodies between the two trees. Asserting "the two bodies differ" would make this case fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the behaviour under test.

expectation.description: the request never settles and the step times out

notes: the image branch of files.download - reply(stream).type(...).bytes(...) with no return and no resolving call, so the deferred is never settled and the request hangs
the branch is chosen by the file document's `type` field, which on this seeded record is the legacy literal image/png
an expected timeout is a RECORDED RESULT, not a failure: it is the only way this branch is captured without hanging the run
against the migrated tree this case is expected to answer 200 with the stream, which is the approved deviation in AAP 0.7

expectedDeviation.baseline: The request never settles: the image branch ends at `.bytes(...)` with no `return` and nothing that resolves the deferred [lib/controllers/files.js:98-100], so the step is recorded as an expected timeout.
expectedDeviation.target: A 200 stream response carrying the file's own mime type and byte length, and NO Content-Disposition - the image branch deliberately omits the header its sibling four lines below sets [lib/controllers/files.js:102-105].
expectedDeviation.reason: An unsettled request is the absence of a response, not a behaviour a client can depend on, so R-d's protection does not attach to it; the intended response is present in the same function for the non-image case; and R-b is unqualified about routes serving.

expectation.description: answers 200 through the fallback rather than 404 or 500

notes: the controller method this route names does not exist, so the response comes entirely from the parser's no-controller fallback, which returns the request.params projection
driven anonymously; this route carries no pre-handlers

expectation.description: both requests redirect to step 1's target, /signup

notes: the fail template for this route is /{formName} and the interpolated value is assigned back onto the parse-time object, so the first validation failure consumes the token for the life of the process

step 1 sends formName=signup and step 2 sends formName=login, both omitting the required email and password; at baseline BOTH redirect to /signup, and a build that redirected step 2 to /login would have fixed a documented quirk
the two Location values must be compared to EACH OTHER, not only to the baseline recording - that comparison is what detects the fix

expectation.description: a real archive response

notes: trinket.downloadPostedZip - reply(readStream).type(application/zip).bytes(...).header(...), resolved by the header call

expectation.description: the aliased slug does not produce a 301

notes: step 1 renames the seeded course, which is what makes its previous slug an alias: the model links the old slug to the course id on save
step 2 addresses the course by that now-aliased slug, which is the branch under test; at baseline the redirect is discarded and the pre value is null, so no 301 is emitted
the slug store runs in-memory because Redis is disabled for the harness, so the alias lives for the lifetime of this server only - which is why the two steps must be one ordered sequence
this sequence CHANGES the seeded course slug and therefore runs in the mutating phase, after every read-only case that addresses it

expectation.description: the callback reports failure while having persisted the user

notes: the profile serves the fixture's unseeded identity "parity-newcomer@example.com", so the callback takes its new-user branch
that branch saves the user and mutates session state, then throws on an undefined variable while flashing the account-created message, so the chain reports the generic authentication failure
the account IS created. The side effect is asserted through the application's own surface after the callback, because a status code alone would record the failure and lose the creation
the derived username for that address is "parity-newcomer-example-com"

expectation.description: step 2 takes the existing-user branch and differs from step 1

notes: the profile serves "parity-existing@example.com", which the seeder does not seed - the fixture's seeding contract asks for it but no such address exists in the seeder, and the alignment call runs only inside the server process

so this is an ORDERED SEQUENCE rather than a single request: step 1 takes the new-user branch and creates the account as a side effect of the quirk itself, and step 2 - the case under test - then finds it and takes the existing-user branch
the user lookup is an $or over email, username and google id, so the account step 1 persists is the one step 2 matches
step 2 is the assertion; step 1 is recorded as its precondition so a reviewer can see where the account came from

expectation.description: the stale session is refused and cleared

notes: step 1 registers a throwaway account, step 2 logs into it, step 3 deletes it through the application's own route, and step 4 is the case under test

the delete route removes the record WITHOUT clearing the session - only logout clears it - so step 4 carries a userId whose document no longer exists, which is the only way this outcome is reachable without touching the database from here
the scheme clears the session and reports "User not found"
no seeded fixture is consumed: the account is created by this sequence for the purpose of being deleted by it

expectation.description: the route is left unsettled, exactly as baseline leaves it

notes: the fixture refuses the connection, emitting an error and never an end
the handler's error listener only logs, so nothing rejects and nothing uploads - the request is left unsettled, which this case records as an expected timeout

this is the log-and-continue disposition: a conversion that turned the logged error into a rejection would answer where baseline hangs, and a conversion that uploaded partial bytes would store an object baseline never stored

expectation.description: the partial content is uploaded and the route answers

notes: the fixture delivers a response and partial bytes, then errors, and then still reaches end - so unlike the refused case the upload DOES start and the partial content is stored
the two failure modes are separate cases because they differ observably, and a conversion that treated them alike would be wrong about one of them

expectation.description: the asset is stored under a name derived from the query-bearing path

notes: the upload filename is derived with a basename over a legacy path field that RETAINS the query string, so the stored filename contains the query - behaviour the target's URL helper preserves deliberately and which therefore has to be exercised rather than assumed
